ABSTRACT 24

Comprehensive clinical history taking is essential for high-quality care. We hypothesized 25

that large language models (LLMs), guided by a structured agentic framework, can 26

efficiently obtain clinically meaningful patient histories. We developed an iterative 27

prompting system that evaluates relevance and completeness across standard history 28

domains and generates targeted follow-up questions until sufficient detail is obtained. 29

We built a patient-facing application and evaluated it using 52 published case reports 30

and 20 constructed clinical scenarios with simulated patient interactions. The framework 31

was implemented using GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, or Grok-3. After each 32

interaction, the system generated an EHR-ready clinical summary, differential diagnosis, 33

and recommended investigations. Across models, relevant history elements were 34

captured with >85% accuracy and F1 scores, as independently assessed by three 35

blinded physicians, and recommended investigations aligned with those used to 36

establish final diagnoses. These findings support the potential of agentic LLM systems 37

for structured clinical history collection and justify prospective clinical evaluation. 38

39

Keywords: Large language models, agentic AI, clinical history-taking, pre-visit 40

workflows, clinical decision support, electronic health records, patient–clinician 41

interaction 42

MAIN TEXT: 44

Clinical history is a foundational pillar of diagnostic reasoning, triage and treatment 45

planning. However, outpatient clinicians frequently operate under substantial time 46

constraints and documentation burden, which can lead to incomplete histories, 47

diagnostic delays and fragmented clinical communication. Systems powered by large 48

language models (LLMs) have therefore emerged as promising tools to augment 49

history-taking by improving both efficiency and patient engagement1,2. 50

Recent studies highlight both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in clinical settings. 51

While state-of-the-art models perform well on medical examination questions and 52

synthetic case vignettes, their performance is less consistent in realistic clinical tasks 53

such as collecting comprehensive patient histories3. For example, general-purpose 54

LLMs have been shown to underperform resident physicians in emergency department 55

scenarios, often producing conservative or insufficiently precise diagnostic, triage, and 56

management recommendations4. By contrast, purpose-built clinical systems that employ 57

structured conversational strategies have demonstrated improved diagnostic dialogue 58

and differential diagnosis generation, in some cases matching or exceeding clinician 59

performance in simulated evaluations5-7. These findings suggest that the limitations of 60

LLMs in history-taking may reflect the design of conversational frameworks rather than 61

intrinsic model capability. 62

As LLM-based systems begin to enter clinical workflows, rigorous methods for 63

evaluating their ability to collect clinically meaningful histories are essential. Prior 64

evaluations indicate that unstructured conversational designs can lead to omissions and 65

variability in collected information8. Additionally in clinical settings, expert-led validation 66

remains the gold standard for assessing AI performance, as human oversight provides a 67

level of contextual scrutiny that autonomous self-evaluation currently cannot replicate. 68

Structured, agentic AI systems that explicitly guide dialogue through modular clinical 69

tasks provide a principled approach to both assessment and improvement9. Moreover, 70

recent advances allow such systems to be deployed within secure, HIPAA-compliant 71

environments, supporting their potential use in healthcare settings10,11. 72

To enable systematic pre-visit history collection, we developed a conversational 73

application that employs a structured, modular prompting framework. The system 74

progresses through the major components of a clinical history taking process in a 75

predefined sequence, including history of present illness, past medical history, 76

medication history, and social and family history. For each section, the agent generates 77

targeted questions, evaluates the clinical relevance of patient responses, records 78

accepted information, produces interim summaries, and determines whether sufficient 79

detail has been obtained for each section or whether additional follow-up questioning is 80

required (Extended Data Fig. 1). Separate interfaces are provided for patients and 81

physicians. Patients engage with a web-based conversational intake interface that 82

supports iterative, context-aware history collection in real time, whereas clinicians 83

review a structured, EHR-ready summary that consolidates the captured history and 84

presents diagnostic impressions and recommended investigations for downstream 85

clinical assessment (Extended Data Fig. 2). The application is deployed as an online 86

system, with access details provided in the Online Content section. 87

Using this framework, we benchmarked three leading LLMs (GPT-4o, Grok-3 and 88

Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite) across fifty-two published clinical case reports drawn from peer- 89

reviewed medical journals, spanning thirteen medical specialties, as well as twenty 90

constructed clinical scenarios designed to represent common outpatient presentations 91

and routine diagnostic decision contexts that are underrepresented in published case 92

reports, which often emphasize rare or atypical conditions (Extended Data Table 1). 93

Simulated patient interactions were conducted by physicians and medical students 94

following the source case descriptions. Independent clinician evaluators from different 95

institutions then assessed the chatbot-generated histories against the corresponding 96

gold-standard case reports using a predefined rubric, with evaluators blinded to model 97

identity. 98

Across the published case reports, all three models demonstrated consistently high 99

performance in structured history collection. Overall F1 score and recall were high and 100

tightly clustered across models, with narrow confidence intervals, indicating stable and 101

reproducible behavior across cases and evaluators (Fig. 1a). These results show that 102

the structured agentic framework enables reliable capture of clinically relevant history 103

elements and minimizes variability associated with free-form conversational designs. 104

Clinician assessments showed modest but consistent agreement in relative model 105

performance across cases (moderate criterion validity ICCs: 0.50–0.58), despite poor 106

inter-rater reliability among clinicians, likely reflecting the inherent subjectivity of flexible, 107

clinician-defined scoring across history components. 108

We next examined performance across individual components of the clinical history. All 109

models showed strong and uniform results across history of present illness, past 110

medical history, medication history, and social and family history, with consistently high 111

section-wise F1 score and recall (Fig. 1b). This indicates that the framework promotes 112

balanced coverage of clinical content rather than selective optimization of a subset of 113

history elements. Case-level section-wise analyses further demonstrated that no single 114

history component systematically underperformed across cases or models, supporting 115

the robustness of section-level performance (Extended Data Fig. 3a). 116

To assess generalizability, we evaluated the same framework on twenty constructed 117

clinical scenarios representing common outpatient presentations with a broader range 118

of presenting complaints, comorbidities, and clinical trajectories. Overall performance on 119

these constructed cases was qualitatively similar to that observed for the published 120

case reports, with high F1 score and recall across all three models and narrow 121

confidence intervals despite increased heterogeneity in case design (Fig. 2a). Section- 122

wise performance across constructed cases remained stable across history 123

components, with variability comparable to that observed in the published case reports 124

(Extended Data Fig. 3b). Together, these findings indicate that the framework 125

generalizes beyond the structure of published case reports and performs robustly 126

across both naturalistic and commonly encountered clinical scenarios. 127

We next evaluated downstream clinical reasoning tasks, specifically generation of a 128

likely diagnosis and identification of clinically important red flags. Across the published 129

case reports, diagnostic performance was moderate for all three models and 130

consistently lower than history collection metrics (Fig. 2b). This finding is expected, as 131

accurate diagnosis often requires integration of physical examination findings, 132

laboratory data, imaging, and disease progression, which were not available to the 133

LLMs. By contrast, performance on red-flag identification was substantially stronger, 134

with all models reliably highlighting major safety concerns (Fig. 2b). 135

Evaluation of the constructed cases yielded a distinct pattern. Diagnostic performance 136

was higher for these scenarios, which were intentionally designed to reflect common 137

clinical presentations that are relatively straightforward to diagnose (Fig. 2c). 138

Identification of red flags remained consistent and within an acceptable range across 139

models, even in cases with overlapping symptom patterns or diagnostic ambiguity (Fig. 140

2c). 141

Finally, pairwise comparison of aggregate history scores revealed broadly concordant 142

performance across models for both published case reports and constructed clinical 143

scenarios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Across the published case reports, Grok 144

demonstrated modest but statistically significant differences relative to GPT and Gemini, 145

whereas no significant difference was observed between Gemini and GPT. In the 146

constructed cases, pairwise differences were smaller and did not consistently reach 147

statistical significance, reflecting increased overlap in model performance across 148

common clinical scenarios. These analyses indicate that while small model-specific 149

differences exist, total history capture is largely comparable across models when 150

deployed within the structured agentic framework. 151

Taken together, these findings demonstrate that a structured agentic framework 152

substantially improves the ability of large language models to collect clinically 153

meaningful patient histories across a wide range of scenarios. Across seventy-two total 154

clinical cases, encompassing both published case reports and constructed clinical 155

scenarios, the system achieved high and stable performance across all major 156

components of the clinical history and reliably identified dangerous conditions requiring 157

consideration. Although diagnostic performance was more heterogeneous as expected 158

when relying on history alone, the framework consistently supported clinically relevant 159

safety assessment. 160

These results have important implications for clinical practice. Automated, structured 161

history collection has the potential to improve completeness of patient information, 162

decrease omissions that contribute to delayed or missed diagnoses and most 163

importantly reduce documentation burden, thereby reducing physician burnout. The 164

observed stability of performance across diverse cases suggests that such systems 165

could function as reliable intake tools in outpatient clinics, telemedicine encounters, and 166

urgent care settings. The modular design of the agentic framework further enables 167

adaptation to specialty-specific workflows and integration with electronic health record 168

systems. 169

This study has several limitations. All encounters were simulated rather than derived 170

from real patient interactions, which may not fully capture the variability of 171

communication observed in clinical practice. In addition, clinician reviewers noted that in 172

a subset of cases, the system did not consistently elicit sex-specific or context- 173

dependent history elements; for example, pregnancy-related questions in young women 174

presenting with abdominal pain. However, this reflects limitations of the current 175

prompting strategy rather than fundamental model capability and could be addressed in 176

future iterations through targeted prompt constraints, rule-based safety checks, or 177

section-specific branching logic. 178

Although more advanced large language models were available at the time of 179

evaluation, we prioritized models with lower inference latency to support responsive, 180

iterative dialogue; more computationally intensive models may improve downstream 181

Finally, the scale of evaluation was constrained by the use of manual clinician review for 183

each generated history. This rigorous assessment approach limited the total number of 184

cases relative to studies that rely on automated self-evaluation by LLMs but ensured 185

clinically meaningful and independent validation of performance. Future studies should 186

evaluate the framework in real-world clinical deployments, incorporate multimodal 187

clinical data such as laboratory results and imaging, and assess generalizability across 188

a broader range of model architectures. 189

METHODS 230

Study Design and Overview 231

We designed a multi-stage evaluation to assess whether a structured agentic artificial 232

intelligence (AI) system can reliably collect pre-visit clinical histories using large 233

language models (LLMs). Three LLMs were evaluated using this agentic framework: 234

GPT-4o, Grok-3, and Gemini-2.5-flash-lite. The study consisted of two components. 235

First, applying each LLM, we evaluated the system on fifty-two published clinical case 236

reports drawn from peer-reviewed journals spanning thirteen medical specialties. 237

Similarly, we evaluated all three LLMs on twenty constructed clinical scenarios designed 238

to represent common outpatient presentations and to complement the breadth of the 239

published cases (Extended Data Table 1). All cases were evaluated using simulated 240

patient–chatbot interactions conducted by physicians and medical students following the 241

source case descriptions. 242

Description of the Agentic AI System 243

The agentic AI system was designed to guide LLMs through a modular, clinically 244

grounded workflow for structured history collection. The system comprises discrete 245

modules for question generation, response validation, short-term and long-term memory 246

management, interim summarization, follow-up question selection, and conversation 247

termination. These modules communicate through explicit internal instructions, allowing 248

fine-grained control over the interaction flow. The system progresses sequentially 249

through the major components of a standard clinical history, including the chief 250

complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, medication history, allergies, 251

social and family history, and review of systems. Within each section, patient responses 252

are evaluated for clinical relevance and completeness before being stored in a 253

structured history state. Interim summaries are generated to maintain coherence and 254

contextual awareness. At the conclusion of each interaction, the system produces an 255

electronic health record (EHR)-compatible clinical summary, a list of likely diagnoses, a 256

list of dangerous diagnoses requiring exclusion, and recommended initial investigations. 257

The agentic control logic was held constant across all evaluations, with only the 258

underlying LLM varied between experiments (Extended Data Fig. 1). 259

Simulated Patient Interactions 260

Simulated patient interactions were conducted by physicians and advanced medical 261

students who assumed the role of the patient while referencing the full content of each 262

case. Participants were instructed to respond conversationally, provide only information 263

contained in the source case, and avoid introducing new details. Each case was 264

evaluated independently with each model. This resulted in 156 total chatbot-generated 265

history transcripts for the 52 published case reports and 60 transcripts for the twenty 266

constructed cases. 267

Reference Standards 268

For published case reports, the gold-standard history and final diagnosis were derived 269

directly from the original publication. For constructed cases, the gold-standard history 270

and diagnosis corresponded to the scenario intentionally designed by the research 271

team. Clinically important red flags were defined as diagnoses or conditions requiring 272

Clinician Scoring Procedure 275

Three trained physicians independently evaluated each chatbot-generated history 276

alongside the corresponding gold-standard history. Scoring was performed using a 277

predefined rubric that assessed the presence and clinical relevance of key history 278

elements within each section of the encounter, including history of present illness, past 279

medical history, medication history, and social and family history (Extended Data Table 280

2). Metrics were computed conditional on sections containing clinically relevant 281

information in the reference case. Reviewers also evaluated system-generated 282

diagnostic suggestions and identification of clinically important red flags relative to the 283

reference answers. All scores were aggregated across reviewers for downstream 284

analysis. 285

Evaluation Metrics 286

Performance was primarily assessed using recall and F1 score, which quantify the 287

completeness and balance of captured clinical information. Metrics were computed for 288

the full clinical history and for individual history sections. For diagnostic performance 289

and red-flag identification, normalized scores ranging from 0 to 1 were computed based 290

on clinician grading. Summary statistics are reported as mean values with 95% 291

confidence intervals across cases and evaluators. 292

Statistical Analysis 293

Scores were aggregated across clinician evaluators for each case prior to analysis. 294

Primary analyses focused on relative model performance rather than absolute score 295

calibration. Between-model comparisons were primarily descriptive. Exploratory 296

pairwise comparisons of aggregate history scores between models were performed 297

using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with corresponding P values reported where 298

applicable (Extended Data Fig. 4). 299

To assess inter-rater reliability and criterion validity, clinician agreement was quantified 300

using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Because clinicians applied 301

individualized scoring scales and weightings across history components, raw scores 302

were first Z-score normalized within each clinician to enable meaningful comparison of 303

relative rankings. Inter-rater reliability was evaluated separately for the original NEJM 304

histories and for each AI model using a two-way random-effects ICC for consistency, 305

averaged across raters (ICC(C,k)). Criterion validity was assessed by comparing each 306

AI model’s normalized scores to the normalized original history scores using a two-way 307

random-effects ICC for consistency, single rater (ICC(C,1)). This approach captures 308

consistency in relative performance while fully accommodating differences in absolute 309

scoring scales and clinician preferences. 310

All statistical analyses and figure generation were performed using R (version 4.5.1). 311

DATA AND CODE AVAILABILITY 318

The datasets generated and analyzed during this study include published clinical case 319

reports and synthesized clinical scenarios. Published case reports are publicly available 320

from their original sources. Synthesized clinical scenarios were constructed by the 321

authors to represent common outpatient presentations and do not contain real patient 322

data; details of cases are provided in Extended Data Table 1. 323

The core conversational agent software used for clinical history collection is subject to a 324

pending patent application and is therefore not publicly available at this time. Code used 325

for data processing, metric computation, statistical analysis, and figure generation will 326

be made publicly available upon publication via a version-controlled GitHub repository. 327
